labs.tagline: A precise snapshot of what is running.
labs.problem: Identify a process, its owner, its parent and its resource usage without guessing.
labs.how: Reads /proc and prints a selected set of processes with chosen columns. Static snapshot, unlike top.

flags.why: Full format with UID, PID, PPID and start time.

labs.sample:
$ ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,pcpu,pmem,etime,cmd --sort=-pcpu | head -4
  PID  PPID USER     STAT %CPU %MEM     ELAPSED CMD
 1204     1 postgres S    12.4  8.1    3-02:11:04 /usr/bin/postgres -D /var/lib/pgsql/data
 1330     1 root     S     1.2  0.4    3-02:11:04 nginx: worker process
 4242     1 svcapp   R    99.0  2.2       00:03:41 /usr/bin/myapp --worker
read: STAT shows state: R running, S sleeping, D uninterruptible IO wait, Z zombie, T stopped.
ELAPSED tells you how long it has run: a 3-minute process at 99% CPU just started, which often means a crash loop.
PPID 1 means it was reparented to systemd/init — its original parent is gone.
%CPU here is an average over the process lifetime, not instantaneous; top shows live usage.
mistakes: Killing a PID without confirming the user and command first.
Forgetting that PIDs are recycled; write down the start time too.
labs.when: First step of any process investigation: identify before acting.

try.scenario: Identify the top CPU consumers and check for zombies or IO-blocked processes on your machine.
try.task: Print the top CPU processes with state and elapsed time, then count processes in D and Z states.
try.command: ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,pcpu,etime,cmd --sort=-pcpu | head -6; echo ---; ps -eo stat | awk 'NR>1 && ($1 ~ /^D/ || $1 ~ /^Z/)' | sort | uniq -c

expected_patterns.label: process rows with a state column
the state census section (even if empty)

try.verdict_ok: You have current process state plus an explicit check for D and Z states.
try.verdict_missing: Paste both sections including the header so the columns are interpretable.

simulate.intro: A service is looping. Read the snapshot.
simulate.terminal:
$ ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,pcpu,etime,cmd --sort=-pcpu | head -3
  PID  PPID USER     STAT %CPU     ELAPSED CMD
 4242     1 svcapp   R    99.0     00:00:12 /usr/bin/myapp --worker
 4243  4242 svcapp   Z     0.0     00:00:09 [myapp] <defunct>

questions.prompt: What is the most likely situation?
options: The process is healthy and simply busy
The worker restarts constantly (12s elapsed at 99% CPU) and one of its children has exited without being reaped
The system is out of memory
questions.explanation: A 12-second-old process at 99% plus a defunct child of that process means a crash/restart loop with unreaped children.

why_wrong.1: The elapsed time is too short for a stable worker.

questions.prompt: Where do you look next for the cause?
options: journalctl -u myapp and the application log for crash or exception output
questions.explanation: A crash loop is diagnosed from logs, not from more process snapshots.

why_wrong.1: The snapshot already told you the shape of the problem.

apply.scenario: `ps` shows a process with PPID 1 that you did not start via systemd.
apply.question: What does that mean?
options: It was necessarily started by systemd
Its original parent exited and it was reparented to PID 1 — it is now effectively unmanaged unless a supervisor adopts it
apply.explanation: Orphaning reparents to init/systemd, which does not mean the process has a unit or a restart policy.

why_wrong.1: PPID 1 is the reparenting result, not proof of a unit.
why_wrong.2: Kernel threads appear with brackets and usually PPID 2.

labs.problem: Stop or reload a process, choosing the least destructive signal that works.
labs.how: Sends a signal to a PID (or a process group). SIGTERM is the default; SIGKILL cannot be caught.

flags.why: Check whether you may signal the PID (permission test).

examples.note: Reload via PID file, where supported.

labs.sample:
$ ps -p 4242 -o pid,stat,cmd
  PID STAT CMD
 4242 S    /usr/bin/myapp --worker
$ kill 4242
$ sleep 2; ps -p 4242 -o pid,stat,cmd
  PID STAT CMD
$ kill -0 4242
kill: (4242): No such process
read: No output from ps -p means the process is gone — the graceful signal worked.
kill -0 is a permission and existence test; it sends nothing.
If the process remains after SIGTERM, read its logs before escalating: it may be blocked in D state, where even SIGKILL waits.
Signalling a process group (negative PID) affects children too — powerful and easy to misuse.
mistakes: Skipping straight to -9 and losing cleanup, leaving stale locks or PID files.
Killing a PID that has already been recycled (you wrote it down minutes ago).
Using kill on a systemd service instead of systemctl, so the unit's restart policy fights you.
labs.when: After identifying the process and confirming no supervised stop is more appropriate.

try.scenario: Practise the graceful-then-forceful sequence on a process you create yourself. Never do this on system processes.
try.task: Start a throwaway sleep, terminate it gracefully, and confirm it is gone.
try.command: sleep 300 & PID=$!; echo "started=$PID"; kill "$PID"; sleep 1; ps -p "$PID" > /dev/null && echo 'still running' || echo 'terminated gracefully'

expected_patterns.label: the PID of the process you created

try.verdict_ok: You signalled a process you own and verified the outcome — the safe, repeatable pattern.
try.verdict_missing: Paste both lines so the signal and the verification are visible.

simulate.intro: A service ignores a normal stop request. Read the sequence.
simulate.terminal:
$ systemctl stop myapp
Job for myapp.service failed because a timeout was exceeded.
$ ps -eo pid,stat,cmd | grep '[m]yapp'
 4242 D    /usr/bin/myapp --worker
$ kill -9 4242
$ ps -p 4242 -o pid,stat
  PID STAT
 4242 D

questions.prompt: Why is the process still there after SIGKILL?
options: It is in uninterruptible sleep (D) waiting on IO, so the signal is not delivered until the syscall returns
questions.explanation: Signal delivery happens on return to user space; a task blocked in the kernel cannot be interrupted.

why_wrong.3: SIGKILL works for any process you may signal, regardless of state.
why_wrong.0: The stat column shows the same PID still blocked.
why_wrong.2: A restart would show a new PID and usually state S/R.

questions.prompt: What is the correct next investigation?
options: Storage: check IO subsystem health and what the process is waiting on (dmesg, /proc/PID/stack, vmstat)
questions.explanation: D state with an unkillable process points at storage or a stuck kernel operation.

why_wrong.0: It has no effect in D state.
why_wrong.3: A reboot may be needed eventually, but only after evidence is captured.

apply.scenario: You must restart a production service. It has a systemd unit with Restart=always.
apply.question: What is the correct action?
options: systemctl restart myapp, so systemd applies the unit's stop signal, timeout and start order
apply.explanation: The unit defines the lifecycle; bypassing it produces a restart race and loses dependency ordering.

why_wrong.2: Skips cleanup and lets the policy restart it unpredictably.
why_wrong.0: Same problem, less forceful, still bypasses the unit.

labs.tagline: Services with a lifecycle, not just processes.
labs.problem: Determine the state of a service, why it failed, what it actually executes, and manage it safely.
labs.how: Client for systemd (PID 1). Units describe how to run something; systemd tracks state, restarts and logs.

flags.why: State, exit code and recent log lines.
The unit file plus drop-ins, in load order.
Effective values: User, ExecStart, Restart, TimeoutStopSec.

examples.note: Is it running and why did it stop?

labs.sample:
$ systemctl status myapp
* myapp.service - My Application
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/myapp.service; enabled; preset: disabled)
     Active: failed (Result: exit-code) since Mon 2026-11-17 09:59:12 UTC; 3min ago
    Process: 4242 ExecStart=/usr/bin/myapp --config /etc/myapp/app.conf (code=exited, status=1/FAILURE)
   Main PID: 4242 (code=exited, status=1/FAILURE)

Nov 17 09:59:12 host myapp[4242]: FATAL: cannot open /etc/myapp/app.conf: Permission denied
read: 'Active: failed (Result: exit-code)' plus the Process line gives you the exit status.
The last log lines in status often contain the actual error — here a permissions problem.
'enabled' means it starts at boot; 'disabled' does not, and 'masked' prevents starting at all.
systemctl cat shows drop-ins that may override what you think the unit says.
mistakes: Reading only the Active line and ignoring the Process/exit code.
Editing the unit and forgetting systemctl daemon-reload.
Using kill instead of systemctl, then being confused by Restart=always.
labs.when: Any service-level problem: not starting, restarting constantly, or behaving differently than manually.

try.scenario: Inspect a real unit on your Fedora machine and extract its effective execution identity.
try.task: Pick a running service, show its status briefly and its effective User/ExecStart.
try.command: SVC=$(systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-legend --no-pager | awk 'NR==3{print $1}'); echo "service=$SVC"; systemctl status "$SVC" --no-pager | head -8; echo ---; systemctl show -p User,Group,ExecStart "$SVC"
try.verdict_ok: You have state plus the effective execution identity — the combination needed to explain most service failures.
try.verdict_missing: Paste the status block and the systemctl show output.

simulate.intro: A service fails immediately after a deploy. Read the evidence.
simulate.terminal:
$ systemctl status myapp --no-pager
* myapp.service - My Application
     Active: failed (Result: exit-code) since Mon 2026-11-17 09:59:12 UTC
    Process: 4242 ExecStart=/usr/bin/myapp --config /etc/myapp/app.conf (code=exited, status=1/FAILURE)

Nov 17 09:59:12 host myapp[4242]: FATAL: cannot open /etc/myapp/app.conf: Permission denied
$ systemctl show -p User,Group myapp
User=svcapp
Group=svcapp
$ ls -l /etc/myapp/app.conf
-rw-r----- 1 root myapp 512 Nov 17 09:58 /etc/myapp/app.conf

options: The service runs as svcapp:svcapp but the file is root:myapp with group read — svcapp is neither owner nor group member
The unit has the wrong ExecStart
questions.explanation: Permission evaluation: owner root (no), group myapp (svcapp is not in it), others (no r). Access denied.

why_wrong.3: ExecStart ran and failed on the file.

options: Add svcapp to the myapp group (or set Group=myapp in the unit) — not chmod 777
questions.explanation: Grant exactly the access needed, through group membership or the unit's Group setting.

why_wrong.3: World-writable config is a security hole.
why_wrong.1: World-readable temp location, and SELinux would likely block it.

apply.scenario: After editing a unit file, `systemctl restart` still uses the old ExecStart.
apply.question: Why?
options: systemd has not reloaded unit definitions — run systemctl daemon-reload
apply.explanation: Unit files are cached; daemon-reload re-reads them and regenerates dependencies.

why_wrong.3: That gives a write error, not a stale unit.
why_wrong.1: Restart does re-read the cached definition.

labs.tagline: The log of everything systemd collected.
labs.problem: Find the error that explains a failure, bounded by unit and time.
labs.how: Queries the systemd journal (binary, indexed by unit, priority, boot and time).

flags.why: How much space the journal takes.

examples.note: Did the kernel kill a process?

labs.sample:
$ journalctl -u myapp --since '10 min ago' --no-pager | tail -6
Nov 17 09:59:12 host systemd[1]: Starting My Application...
Nov 17 09:59:12 host myapp[4242]: FATAL: cannot open /etc/myapp/app.conf: Permission denied
Nov 17 09:59:12 host systemd[1]: myapp.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
Nov 17 09:59:12 host systemd[1]: myapp.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.
read: Lines from the unit appear with the process name in brackets; lines from systemd itself are labelled systemd[1].
The 'Failed with result' line summarises why systemd gave up (exit-code, timeout, signal).
Use -k for kernel messages: OOM kills and interface flaps never appear in the unit's own log.
Bounding with --since makes the output readable and the evidence citable.
mistakes: Dumping the entire journal and drowning in noise.
Looking only at the application's log file when the failure was a kernel OOM kill.
Assuming the journal has everything — a unit can redirect StandardOutput elsewhere.
labs.when: Immediately after systemctl status suggests a failure, and for any 'why did it die' question.

try.scenario: Collect this boot's error-level messages, bounded, and check for kernel events.
try.task: Show errors from this boot, then the last kernel lines.
try.command: journalctl -b -p err --no-pager | tail -12; echo ---; journalctl -k -b --no-pager | tail -6

expected_patterns.label: an error-level message or an explicit empty marker

try.verdict_ok: You have bounded error-level evidence and the kernel view, which is where OOM kills and link events appear.
try.verdict_missing: Paste the journal lines; if nothing is there, an explicit marker is acceptable evidence too.

simulate.intro: A service died overnight. Find the cause in the journal.
simulate.terminal:
$ journalctl -k -b --no-pager | grep -i -m2 'memory\|killed'
Nov 16 23:41:02 host kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 4242 (java) total-vm:8123456kB
Nov 16 23:41:02 host kernel: oom_reaper: reaped process 4242 (java)
$ systemctl status myapp --no-pager | head -4
* myapp.service - My Application
     Active: failed (Result: signal) since Sun 2026-11-16 23:41:02 UTC
    Process: 4242 ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/myapp/app.jar (code=killed, signal=KILL)

options: The kernel OOM killer due to memory pressure — evidence is in the kernel journal, not the app log
questions.explanation: signal=KILL plus the kernel's OOM line identifies the kernel as the killer.

why_wrong.2: Possible in principle, but the OOM record is direct evidence.
why_wrong.3: That yields exit-code, not signal KILL.
why_wrong.1: That does not terminate a JVM.

questions.prompt: What is the correct mitigation path?
options: Investigate memory usage and limits (heap sizing, cgroup limits) rather than simply restarting
questions.explanation: The cause is memory demand versus available memory or cgroup limits; sizing and limits are the durable fix.

why_wrong.2: Swap can help but masks the sizing problem and hurts latency.

apply.scenario: A unit's own log file shows nothing at the time it stopped.
apply.question: Where do you look?
options: journalctl -k -b and the unit's journal in the same time window, including signal/exit information from systemd
apply.explanation: Kernel and systemd records capture kills, OOM, dependency failures and timeouts that the application cannot log.

why_wrong.2: Re-reading the same empty file adds nothing.
